content: Psoriasis is a chronic autoimmune skin disease characterized by accelerated skin cell proliferation leading to red, scaly plaques primarily on the elbows, knees, scalp, and trunk. It results from a complex interplay of genetic, immunological, and environmental factors that disrupt normal skin cell turnover and immune regulation. Major types include plaque psoriasis, guttate, inverse, pustular, and erythrodermic forms, each with unique clinical features. Synonyms sometimes used include 'psoriatic disease' encompassing skin and joint involvement, notably psoriatic arthritis. Diagnosis is mainly clinical, supported by characteristic lesion morphology; definitive tests are limited. Treatments span topical agents, phototherapy, systemic immunomodulators, and biologics targeting specific immune pathways such as TNF-α and IL-17. Practical significance includes management of symptoms, improving quality of life, and reducing risk of comorbidities such as cardiovascular disease. Limitations exist in predicting individual treatment response and cure; psoriasis is generally chronic with fluctuating course. Safety aspects include monitoring for adverse effects of systemic therapies and managing psychological impact. Awareness of misconceptions such as infectiousness and lifestyle blame improves patient care and social support.

content: Psoriasis is a chronic, immune-mediated inflammatory skin disorder characterized by the rapid proliferation of keratinocytes resulting in thickened, scaly, erythematous plaques on the skin. It is considered an autoimmune disease involving dysregulation of the innate and adaptive immune systems, particularly T-helper 1 (Th1) and T-helper 17 (Th17) pathways.

content: Psoriasis affects approximately 2–3% of the global population and can lead to significant physical discomfort, psychological distress, and impaired quality of life. Effective management improves symptoms, reduces complications, and supports overall wellbeing.

chunk_title: Overview of Psoriasis: Definition and Types
content: Psoriasis is a chronic autoimmune skin condition defined by accelerated skin cell turnover causing raised, red, scaly plaques. The most common type is plaque psoriasis, accounting for about 80–90% of cases. Other forms include guttate psoriasis (small drop-like lesions, often triggered by infections), inverse psoriasis (affects skin folds without scaling), pustular psoriasis (characterized by white pustules on red skin), and erythrodermic psoriasis (widespread redness and scaling). Each type varies in appearance, severity, and triggers.

content: Psoriasis results from immune system dysregulation involving T-cells, dendritic cells, and proinflammatory cytokines such as tumor necrosis factor alpha (TNF-α), interleukin-17 (IL-17), and interleukin-23 (IL-23). This immune activation leads to excessive keratinocyte proliferation and impaired differentiation, creating thickened plaques. Genetic factors influence immune responses, and environmental triggers can precipitate or worsen lesions.

review_status: AI draft - scientific, clinical, and editorial review required
content: Genetic susceptibility is evidenced by familial clustering and identified psoriasis-associated genes such as HLA-C*06:02 and other loci related to immune regulation. Environmental risk factors include infections (e.g., streptococcal throat infection triggering guttate psoriasis), stress, smoking, alcohol use, obesity, medications (lithium, beta-blockers), and skin injury (Koebner phenomenon). These factors interact to influence disease onset and exacerbation.

content: Psoriasis presents as well-demarcated, erythematous plaques with silvery scale, commonly on extensor surfaces, scalp, and lower back. Patients may experience itching, pain from skin fissures, and nail changes like pitting or onycholysis. In psoriatic arthritis, joint pain, swelling, and stiffness occur, often involving distal interphalangeal joints and the spine.

content: Diagnosis of psoriasis is primarily clinical, based on typical lesion morphology and distribution. Skin biopsy may be used in atypical cases to confirm diagnosis. Laboratory tests are generally unnecessary but may assess inflammation or comorbidities. Assessment tools like the Psoriasis Area and Severity Index (PASI) quantify disease severity to guide treatment.

content: Psoriasis management depends on severity, disease extent, and patient preference. Topical therapies include corticosteroids, vitamin D analogs (calcipotriene), and calcineurin inhibitors. Phototherapy (UVB, PUVA) is effective for moderate disease. Systemic treatments include methotrexate, cyclosporine, acitretin, and biologics targeting TNF-α, IL-17, or IL-23 pathways. Treatment goals are to reduce lesions, improve quality of life, and minimize adverse effects.

content: Lifestyle modifications, such as maintaining a healthy weight, quitting smoking, moderating alcohol intake, and stress reduction, can help manage psoriasis. Skin moisturization and avoiding triggers like skin trauma or infections are recommended. Patient education enhances adherence and self-care.

content: Psoriasis is linked to increased risk for psoriatic arthritis, cardiovascular disease, metabolic syndrome, depression, and inflammatory bowel disease. This systemic inflammatory state necessitates comprehensive care beyond skin lesions, including screening and management of associated conditions.

review_status: AI draft - scientific, clinical, and editorial review required
content: Safety monitoring is crucial, especially with systemic therapies and biologics that can suppress the immune system, increasing risk of infections and malignancy. Regular blood tests assess liver and kidney function. Awareness of medication side effects, drug interactions, and patient vaccination status improves safety.

content: Psoriasis is not contagious and cannot be transmitted through touch or sharing personal items. It is a medical disorder, not caused by poor hygiene or lifestyle choices alone. Many patients face stigma or misunderstanding, underscoring the importance of public education to dispel myths and support affected individuals.

content: Psoriasis often affects mental health, causing anxiety, depression, and social isolation. Visible and symptomatic disease can impact self-esteem and daily activities. Psychological support, counseling, and patient support groups are important adjuncts to medical treatment.
